evidenceBlocks.sectionReference: Areas of higher risk and exposure
evidenceBlocks.extractedText: Some firms had also set limits to the value of gifts and entertainment received from an individual firm or its employees within a calendar year.
Firms generally maintained gifts and entertainment registers which recorded gifts and hospitality given to third parties.

These included details on value, recipient, business purpose and approval status.   The strongest arrangements supplemented this with compliance oversight and documented justifications for providing hospitality.

While some firms were generally able to show evidence that gifts and entertainment had been approved and recorded, there was less consistent evidence of how the firms assessed and managed the conflicts of interest arising from them.

Registers did not always document the specific conflicts considered, the rationale for concluding that they had been appropriately managed, or how the information was used to support ongoing monitoring and challenge.
Our rules on inducements relating to MiFID business can be found in COBS 2.3A and in article 24 of the Level 2 regulation for AIFMs.
The FSA published a report (PDF) , in 2012, that reviewed how firms managed gifts and entertainment in public markets.
In 2016, we published the findings of a thematic review on the benefits firms conducting MiFID business provided and received, relating to carrying out retail investment regulated activities.

Firms should maintain gifts and entertainment frameworks that are proportionate to the nature, scale and complexity of their business.   We expect firms to demonstrate that controls are not only documented in policies and procedures but are operating effectively in practice.

With such diversity of business models, product offerings, investment strategies and ownership structures across private markets firms, our review focused on a number of recurring conflict types that arise throughout the investment lifecycle.
We assessed how firms identified, managed and oversaw them.
Conflicts can arise during deal sourcing.
These include biased referrals, hidden incentives, related party transactions, and opportunities where a firm or its affiliates have an interest on both sides of a transaction.

If a firm doesn’t identify and managed them, these conflicts can influence which opportunities it pursues and how it assesses them.   Early disclosure and independent screening can manage or prevent conflicted deals from entering the pipeline.
Firms with stronger arrangements embedded conflicts identification into origination and approval processes.
Potential conflicts were assessed at the earliest stages of deal origination through conflict screening, active deal lists, non-disclosure agreement (NDA) stage reviews.
One firm checked for overlapping mandates, competing investor interests, related-party relationships and information-sharing risks before opportunities progressed.
Legal and Compliance were often engaged before NDAs were signed.

This enabled potential conflicts to be identified, challenged and mitigated before opportunities progressed further.   Early-stage reviews helped firms determine whether transactions should proceed before committing significant resources and whether additional controls were required.
Weaker practice involved formal conflict assessments not being consistently undertaken before NDAs were signed, resulting in greater reliance on investment professionals’ judgement at the outset.
Firms with stronger frameworks had embedded conflicts management within formal decision-making and oversight processes.

They reviewed opportunities through oversight forums such as pipeline reviews, stock meetings, steering committees and investment screening committees.   They set clear roles for their second-line functions throughout the process, including the application of consistent thresholds and different escalation routes depending on where conflicts arose.

These were supported by eligibility screening, conflict-clearance processes and documented rationale and challenge.   Together these measures helped ensure that investment decisions aligned with investors’ interests and were not unduly influenced by commercial, fundraising or capital deployment pressures.   Weaker arrangements engaged legal and compliance functions later in the process, either following referrals from the first line or through retrospective reviews once transactions had progressed to the later stages of decision-making.

Weak information controls can allow material non-public information to flow between deal teams, trading desks, or affiliated businesses, potentially influencing investment decisions or trading activity.
It can also give rise to multi-fund investment conflicts, or the misuse of material non-public information.
Firms we saw with the best practice had clear physical, organisational and system-based separation through information barriers.

These arrangements often included zoning teams into separate areas with gated access to maintain confidentiality between asset classes.   Firms also used digital permissions to separate asset classes or strategies.
This prevented staff servicing one asset class from accessing documentation relating to another.
Firms with affiliated banks or insurance companies had physical barriers between their private markets and banking or insurance businesses.
These group-wide controls were particularly important given the risks associated with price-sensitive or confidential information.

Stronger arrangements had active compliance involvement in monitoring and surveillance, applying clear restrictions around information sharing under NDAs, the establishment of information trees and chaperones for discussions that risked crossing information barriers.   This helped firms identify and manage potential links between confidential information received during one opportunity and subsequent investment activity, including where the original opportunity did not progress.
The less effective arrangements we saw relied heavily on training, informal zoning of teams, and little monitoring to ensure the controls were operating effectively.
Controls depended more on individual judgement and staff awareness and there was limited second-line oversight or assurance that confidential information was appropriately contained.
This was particularly relevant where firms operated multiple strategies across the capital stack.
Unfair allocation decisions across different funds, mandates and investment vehicles are likely to disadvantage certain investors.
Firms must balance the competing interests of different investors to demonstrate that they have allocated opportunities fairly and consistently.
Firms typically considered allocation as part of the investment decision-making process, or as a subsequent step once an investment was deemed suitable.
Those with stronger approaches had clearly documented allocation frameworks supported by predefined allocation criteria.

They used pro-rata methodologies for oversubscribed opportunities and supplemented these formulaic approaches with documented rationale explaining how they had considered investor fairness in the specific circumstances of the transaction.   They typically assessed allocation decisions against factors such as investment strategy, mandate suitability, portfolio construction and investor objectives.
Governance committees also provided oversight when conflicts arose and exceptions were made to policy.

Several firms maintained dedicated allocation committees, memoranda and periodic reviews of outcomes giving them greater assurance that competing investor interests had been balanced appropriately.   In weaker approaches, investment teams exercised broad discretion when allocating opportunities between competing mandates.
They had allocation policies but less prescriptive governance arrangements.
Allocation decisions relied on judgement across multiple factors rather than a clearly defined methodology.
This made it harder for allocation outcomes to be independently and systematically challenged and consistently applied.
Connected or multi-party transactions involve multiple funds, investor groups or affiliated parties whose interests may not align.

This creates conflict risks where decisions on pricing, valuation, allocation, timing or terms could advantage one party at the expense of another.   Conflicts in valuations can be particularly acute where firms have discretion in the valuation of fund assets.

In these circumstances, firms may have an incentive to bias valuations for their own benefit at the expense of investors.   These risks can arise in situations such as fund-to-fund transactions, continuation vehicles, warehousing arrangements, related-party and affiliated transactions, secondary transactions and fund wind-downs.   The stronger approaches we saw recognised the risks posed by these transactions and reflected them explicitly within their conflict frameworks, governance arrangements and escalation processes.

They enhanced governance for related-party, affiliated, cross-fund and continuation transactions were typically subject to enhanced governance, conflict-clearance processes and additional oversight beyond standard business-as-usual approvals.   They used separate decision-making teams and processes to represent the potentially competing interests of different investors involved in a transaction.

For example, where different investors were effectively on both sides of a transaction, firms commissioned separate independent valuations from different agents to support transaction pricing.   Stronger firms also undertook compliance monitoring and thematic reviews to assess whether controls were operating effectively in practice.
These reviews also considered whether conflicts arising from broader group structures were being appropriately managed.

They supplemented these arrangements with LPAC engagement, either through consent or by providing timely disclosure where appropriate.   In end-of-fund situations, stronger firms specifically considered conflicts arising from extensions, liquidations, secondary transactions and distressed scenarios within formal governance frameworks.

These situations were subject to additional review, challenge and escalation to Realisation Committees, LPACs or other governance bodies.   By contrast, weak arrangements relied heavily on existing practices to oversee conflicts and used standard fund-specific thresholds for engagement with LPs or LPACs.
There was often only limited escalation where transactions fell within established risk appetites or policy thresholds.
As a result, these firms relied primarily on first-line judgement and management approvals, and fairness considerations were often discussed only at a high level.
In one case, a firm told us that an affiliated party had sought to circumvent the firm’s internal processes.

Firms with poor approaches were also less able to evidence how they had balanced competing investor interests, how they had assessed transaction pricing fairly, or show that potential conflicts had not influenced decision-making.   We also observed examples where the same individuals remained involved on both sides of transactions and where committee memberships overlapped.
Cross-fund transactions and continuation vehicles create conflicts as the firm sits on both sides of the transaction.
This can lead to harm for one set of investors.

Harm can arise, for example, when determining the sale price, the timing of the sale, or the terms on which an asset is transferred from an older fund to a new vehicle.   Some firms recognised these transactions as elevated conflict-risk events.
They explicitly identified conflicts arising from cross-fund and continuation transactions within their frameworks.
Related governance and escalation processes also reflected these risks.

Better approaches maintained clear separation between investment functions and transaction oversight.   This included independent valuations, independent challenge, and clear segregation between buy-side and sell-side decision-makers.
LPACs were also engaged where appropriate, either through consent processes or timely disclosure.
One firm would commission independent valuations for buy-side and sell-side funds, to support transaction pricing.
The weaker arrangements we saw heavily relied on existing governance processes, disclosure or investor consent without substantive independent challenge.
These firms were unable to demonstrate how they had fairly balanced competing interests of different investors.

Governance arrangements were often less developed and buy- and sell-side funds would often rely on the same independent valuation and seek endorsement from the same committee, with largely the same composition, albeit in different sittings.
We were concerned to find that one firm did not follow its established governance processes in a particularly conflicted transaction.

Poor alignment of interests between managers and investors can create incentives that increase the risk of poor outcomes, even in the absence of a direct conflict.   Stronger firms’ arrangements showed clear alignment between manager and investor interests, typically supported through meaningful General Partner (‘GP’) commitments invested alongside clients’ money.

These firms also operated governance arrangements that sought to identify and manage situations where fees, expenses, fundraising activity, capital deployment pressures and other commercial incentives could influence decision-making.   They supplemented this with transaction reviews, governance committee scrutiny and enhanced transparency and oversight mechanisms, including LPAC engagement.
This helped provide greater assurance that investor interests were considered when making decisions that could otherwise be influenced by commercial objectives.
Many firms demonstrated broadly aligned structures, with governance over fees, expenses, allocations and investor reporting.
Weaker firms provided less evidence of how they sought to align GP interests with those of investors.
In some cases, investor alignment was asserted rather than demonstrated through governance, oversight and monitoring.

evidenceBlocks.extractedText: By contrast, weaker practices had less developed governance arrangements for the provision and oversight of MFNs and side letters across products or investor groups.   Where preferential rights were granted, these firms relied more heavily on fund-document disclosure and did not consistently demonstrate that they had systematically assessed their cumulative impact on other investors.
Poor disclosure of conflicts, or potential conflicts, can leave investors unable to assess whether their interests are being fairly protected.

Timely and transparent disclosure is essential to preserve investor trust and support informed decision-making.   The firms we saw with stronger arrangements treated disclosure as a supplementary control rather than a substitute for conflict management.
They prioritised avoiding conflicts or if not possible, taking steps to mitigate and manage them before considering disclosure.
Disclosure was often proactive and timely, and they engaged investors and LPACs early enough to provide meaningful challenge and influence outcomes.

They included clear escalation routes beyond conflict committees to LPACs, and reported transparently on conflicted transactions, with regular investor engagement and ad hoc communications where required.
Some firms were willing to exceed minimum contractual disclosure obligations where they considered that perceived conflict risks were high.
The weaker frameworks we saw relied on disclosure requirements in existing fund documentation as part of their approach to managing conflicts.
They did not always demonstrate robust underlying governance or independent challenge in the oversight of conflicts.
LPAC engagement was often ad hoc, inconsistent or triggered only where legally required.

Escalation thresholds were unclear, and there was limited evidence that investor challenge affected outcomes.   Firms with less effective arrangements lacked systematic approaches for determining when to make disclosures or relied on quarterly reporting cycles rather than timely event-driven communication.
There was also limited evidence that disclosures were delivered early enough to influence decision-making.

evidenceBlocks.extractedText: Throughout the investment lifecycle, we expect firms to maintain effective arrangements to identify, record, manage and monitor conflicts of interest.

evidenceBlocks.extractedText: The specific controls required will vary by business model, product and activity, but firms should be able to demonstrate that they identify conflicts early, subject them to appropriate oversight and challenge, and that their decisions balance competing investor interests.

evidenceBlocks.sectionReference: Managing conflicts throughout the investment lifecycle

We expect firms to consider the findings from this review and identify any gaps in their approach to identifying, assessing and managing conflicts of interest.

In particular, firms should assess whether their conflicts frameworks, governance arrangements and controls remain proportionate to the nature, scale and complexity of their activities and whether they continue to support fair investor outcomes.

A key theme arising from this review was that conflicts management arrangements had not always evolved in line with changes in firms' business models, ownership structures, product offerings and activities.
As private markets continue to grow, innovate and broaden participation, firms should expect the number and significance of conflicts to evolve.
Firms should therefore view conflicts management as a dynamic capability that develops alongside their business, rather than a static compliance framework.
They should not assume that arrangements developed for simpler business models will remain effective as the nature, scale and complexity of their activities change.
As private markets continue to evolve, effective conflicts management will become increasingly important to supporting fair investor outcomes and maintaining confidence in the sector.

Where conflicts are not identified and managed effectively, investors may be exposed to unfair treatment, inappropriate allocation decisions, valuation concerns, preferential treatment of certain investors or other outcomes that undermine confidence in firms and private market investing more broadly.
We recognise the diversity of firms operating in private markets, including differences in scale, business models and activities.
Not all findings will be relevant to every firm.
Nor do we prescribe a particular business model, ownership structure or level of inherent conflicts risk.
However, firms should be able to identify, assess and manage the conflicts arising from their activities and maintain governance and controls commensurate with those risks.
